summary: Describes IAX, the Inter-Asterisk eXchange protocol, an application-layer protocol for creating, modifying, and ending multimedia sessions, mostly VoIP calls. It was created by the open source community for the Asterisk PBX and handles both call control and media in one protocol. This is an informational document, later updated by RFC 8996.

eli5.summary: Many phone systems use one channel for dialing and another for voice. IAX puts both in one stream, so it is easier to get through home networks.

questions: what is the difference between iax and sip
subtitle: A compact VoIP protocol that carries call setup and voice together over one UDP port.

tldr.problem: Voice-over-IP systems usually split signaling and media across several protocols and ports, which adds header overhead and makes NAT traversal and firewall management harder.
tldr.mechanism: IAX is a binary protocol that multiplexes signaling and many media streams over a single UDP port, 4569, using reliable Full Frames for control and small unreliable Mini Frames for voice.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document from the Independent Submission stream, published at the RFC Editor's discretion, and it has since been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5456 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 8996. It was published at the RFC Editor's discretion and is not an Internet Standard.

sections.title: What IAX Is For
sections.content:
IAX (Inter-Asterisk eXchange) is an application-layer control and media protocol for creating, modifying and ending multimedia sessions over IP. It was created through an open source process for the Asterisk PBX and is aimed mainly at VoIP calls. The RFC describes Version 2; Version 1 used a different port and was not widely deployed.

Where SIP and similar protocols leave the media to another protocol such as RTP, IAX does both jobs itself. It multiplexes signaling and several media streams over one UDP association between two hosts, always on the well-known UDP port 4569. Because everything for a call travels the same point-to-point path, NAT traversal is simpler.

The RFC is frank about the costs. Codecs are chosen by a 32-bit mask, so they must be defined in the protocol and the number of simultaneous codecs is limited. A single well-known port is an easier target for denial-of-service attacks. Traffic is typically sent through a central server, which limits scalability, although IAX can now split media from signaling.
sections.eli5: IAX is like a walkie-talkie that uses one channel for both saying 'ring ring' and talking. Only one channel means fewer things that can go wrong.

sections.title: Registration
sections.content:
For one peer to call another it needs the other's network address. IAX offers an optional registration facility: a registrant tells a registrar where it can be reached. A registrant may implement only its half, for example an analog telephone adapter.

The registrant sends REGREQ with its username and a refresh period. If the registrar wants authentication it answers REGAUTH, listing the methods it accepts, and the registrant resends REGREQ with credentials. Success ends with REGACK, which carries the apparent address and should carry the refresh time. If no refresh time is sent, both peers MUST assume a default expiry of 60 seconds. The registrar may send REGREJ at any point, and the registrant can end a registration early with REGREL.

Two authentication methods are described. MD5 uses a challenge and an MD5 sum, but both ends still need plaintext access to the secret. RSA lets one side prove knowledge with a public and private key pair; private keys SHOULD always be 3DES encrypted. Registrants SHOULD renew at random intervals to avoid network congestion, and the registrar MUST invalidate a registration that is not renewed in time.
sections.eli5: Registering is like telling the post office your new address. You show an ID if they ask, and you have to keep telling them or they forget.

sections.title: Setting Up and Ending a Call Leg
sections.content:
A call is built from call legs, and IAX sets up one or more of them. Each leg is labeled with a pair of call numbers, one chosen by each end. A peer starts a leg by sending NEW with a version information element first, normally followed by the called number or context. The receiver MUST answer with one of REJECT, AUTHREQ, ACCEPT, or HANGUP, though REJECT is preferred to HANGUP at that point.

If the caller is challenged with AUTHREQ it SHOULD reply with AUTHREP carrying credentials. After ACCEPT the leg is in the Linked state, and the called side goes on to send PROCEEDING, RINGING, BUSY or ANSWER depending on the called party.

IAX is also peer-to-peer in a useful way. If two adjacent legs both use IAX and a middle peer does not need to stay in the path, it can supervise a path change that removes itself. The RFC says the change is not made until every peer in the new path confirms it can communicate properly.
sections.eli5: To start a call you knock (NEW), the other side says come in, show ID, or go away. Once they let you in, you hear ringing until someone picks up.

sections.title: Frames: Full, Mini and Meta
sections.content:
The frame is the basic unit of IAX. Full Frames carry signaling and are sent reliably, so each needs an acknowledgment. Their standard header is 12 octets: an F bit set to 1, a 15-bit source call number, an R retransmission bit, a 15-bit destination call number, a 32-bit time-stamp in milliseconds, 8-bit outbound and inbound sequence numbers, a frame type, a C bit and a 7-bit subclass.

Mini Frames carry only voice on an established call and are sent unreliably, because lost voice frames are too old to be useful by the time they could be resent. Their header is 4 octets and holds the low 16 bits of the time-stamp. That value wraps after 65.536 seconds, at which point a Full Frame SHOULD be sent to resynchronize. Meta Frames are recognizable because their first 16 bits are all zero, and they carry video or trunked media.

The RFC defines ten frame types, such as DTMF, voice, video, control, IAX control, text, image, HTML and comfort noise. The text works out the overhead for 8 kbit/s voice with 20 ms packets: IAX adds 4 bytes (20%) to most voice packets, where RTP adds 12 bytes (60%).
sections.eli5: Important messages are registered letters that need a signature. Voice is a quick postcard with a tiny stamp, and it is fine if one gets lost.

sections.title: Reliability, Trunking, NAT and Encryption
sections.content:
Reliable messages are counted per call. Every reliable message increments the outgoing count, except ACK, INVAL, TXCNT, TXACC and VNAK. A message that arrives out of order MUST be ignored and answered with VNAK. The retransmission timer starts at twice the round-trip time measured from the last PING/PONG and grows exponentially up to a limit of 10 seconds. After a locally configured number of retries (default 4) without an acknowledgment, the call leg SHOULD be considered unusable and the call MUST be torn down.

Trunking lets several calls between the same two peers share one packet, which means fewer packets in total. A trunk frame has one header and a 32-bit time-stamp, followed by each call's source number, length and media data. The second trunking method keeps each call's Mini Frame time-stamp, at a cost of 2 more octets per call, so jitter buffers get better timing.

On NAT, the single port means a server behind a gateway needs little effort. Several servers behind one gateway generally each need a different UDP port. IAX can encrypt a call with AES (Rijndael, a 128-bit block cipher). The caller asks for encryption in the NEW, the callee agrees in its AUTHREQ, and from then on all messages MUST be encrypted. The key is the 128-bit MD5 digest of the challenge joined with a shared password, and only the data portion is encoded.
sections.eli5: If a message does not get an answer, IAX asks again a few times and then gives up. Sending many calls in one big envelope saves stamps, and a secret code can keep the call private.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says IAX is simpler to secure than more general VoIP protocols, but still difficult. Earlier versions allowed cleartext passwords, and that has been eliminated in favor of MD5 or RSA. Servers use random challenges, which makes replay highly unlikely. The protocol does permit a server to skip the challenge, which the RFC calls not recommended and inherently insecure.

Call details (who is calling whom) are sent unencrypted even when the call is encrypted. Without encryption, audio and video are easy to intercept, and a man-in-the-middle could insert, delete or alter messages. Registration errors return distinct cause codes, so an attacker may learn which users exist. Denial of service can come from bogus requests or from attacks on an existing call, which need the attacker to follow the sequence numbers.

The RFC adds that lower-layer security, DTLS or IPsec, would address many of these problems.
sections.eli5: A secret handshake keeps strangers from joining your call. But anyone listening can still see who is calling whom unless you lock the whole conversation.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Set to 1 for a Full Frame.

fields.name: Source Call Number
fields.desc: Number the sender uses for this call.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Set to 1 when the frame is a retransmission.

fields.name: Destination Call Number
fields.desc: Number the sender uses for the call at the remote peer.

fields.name: Time-stamp
fields.desc: Milliseconds since the first transmission of the call.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: If 1, the subclass is read as a power of 2.
